abstract:
Adverse drug-drug interactions (DDIs) cause preventable hospitalizations, but exhaustive experimental screening of all drug pairs is infeasible. Many computational predictors rely on small-molecule structural representations, limiting their direct applicability to biologic therapeutics. We present a structure-agnostic framework that combines semantic representations derived from Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) with graph-derived topology from a Drug-Target-Protein knowledge graph constructed from DrugBank and UniProt. We further examine how MeSH annotation depth is associated with predictive performance.
In transductive evaluation, latent gated fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.988 and improved mean AUROC and F1 over MeSH-only across all six interaction categories. Improvements in AUROC, F1, and precision remained significant after Holm correction for Low-Mid, Mid-Mid, and Mid-Deep interactions, with the largest mean AUROC gain in Low-Mid (+0.0304). In seen-unseen inductive evaluation, each test pair contained one held-out drug and one seen drug, and all DDI edges were excluded from the feature graphs. Fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.937, exceeding MeSH-only by 0.045; this improvement remained significant after Holm correction. Mean AUROC gains occurred across all six categories, with recurring improvements in Low-Mid ( + 0.063) and Mid-Mid ( + 0.053) that reached nominal significance, although the inductive category-level evidence remained exploratory.
MeSH annotation depth is associated with systematic variation in DDI prediction performance that aggregate evaluation can obscure. Recurring gains for Low-Mid and Mid-Mid interactions across evaluation settings support the predictive benefit of combining MeSH semantics with graph-derived topology, with additional transductive evidence for Mid-Deep interactions. The framework provides a common, structure-agnostic representation compatible with both small-molecule and biologic therapeutics and supports first-pass DDI prioritization for subsequent expert assessment.
Not applicable.
